structure.title: Marriage as negotiation
structure.text: Competing suitors and a father's conditions connect courtship to money, household authority, and a sister's prospects.

structure.title: Conduct under pressure
structure.text: Petruchio's methods make speech, appetite, and public obedience contested terrain. The apparent terms of agreement require scrutiny.

people.name: Katherina
people.text: The sharp-tongued elder daughter of a rich Paduan, known through the town for her temper, whom no one wants to marry.

people.name: Petruchio
people.text: A gentleman from Verona who has come to Padua to marry money, and is not put off by anything he hears about Katherina.

people.name: Bianca
people.text: Katherina's sweet-mannered sister, courted by several suitors, who cannot marry until a husband is found for Katherina.

context.title: Consent and performance
context.text: Agreement spoken under material pressure may have several meanings. The play's comedy does not remove the need to examine the conditions of speech.

context.title: A disputed comedy
context.text: Performance choices can alter how sincerity, irony, and coercion appear. No stage interpretation makes the difficult actions cease to be present.

notice.text: Notice control of food, sleep, and clothing.
notice.why: Domestic authority works through bodily needs.

notice.text: Compare public declarations with private encounters.
notice.why: An audience changes the stakes of obedience.

opening: Petruchio comes to Padua looking for a wealthy wife and hears of a woman everyone else considers impossible. Katherina refuses the sweetness expected of her, and he announces that he knows how to handle that. Their verbal sparring becomes a contest in which marriage gives one participant control over food, sleep, and the terms of reality. Shakespeare's comedy is funny, uncomfortable, and fiercely disputed because its central bargain is so exposed: what will a household do to obtain the appearance of a woman's willing obedience?
